This result is called the **multivariable chain rule**." :tutorial/id #uuid "80ad8a26-7d43-52d6-b0ba-e1d04283e5ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4957 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "03fe551f-81c6-5c42-9baf-d6d12895ab47" :step/math-academy-id 30893 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167573}} {:db/id 17592186167573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166747 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166585 :question/id #uuid "285e2f4a-e8d0-5f5e-a2d2-fe5ba8476358" :question/math-academy-id "e-8256"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ed13b87-51ab-547d-a9ed-960eda7db24e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048707}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167326} {:db/id 17592186167331} {:db/id 17592186284666} {:db/id 17592186360551} {:db/id 17592186360552} {:db/id 17592186360553} {:db/id 17592186360554} {:db/id 17592186360555} {:db/id 17592186360556} {:db/id 17592186360557} {:db/id 17592186383607} {:db/id 17592186385838}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable"} :step/id #uuid "a6ab275a-61df-5648-811a-176fda344fe5" :step/math-academy-id 30861 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167697}} {:db/id 17592186167697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168088 :tutorial/content "There is a special case of the multivariable chain rule when $f=f(x,y)$ and $y=g(x).$ 

Notice that $x$ is an independent variable here. Therefore, the chain rule becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}}_{⏟}}_{1}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "44effd03-02e7-5eb1-8732-ee1522afa147" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5184 :tutorial/title "A Special Case of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "fdc61eff-9eab-552e-9092-f4040bdff21a" :step/math-academy-id 32539 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167574}} {:db/id 17592186167574 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166748 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166586 :question/id #uuid "7da1ada0-43e5-5807-b2c2-2a254a76cf27" :question/math-academy-id "e-8257"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1457941c-efa8-556f-9df7-3c5ae7b44ced" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167327} {:db/id 17592186167332} {:db/id 17592186284667} {:db/id 17592186360558} {:db/id 17592186360566} {:db/id 17592186360568} {:db/id 17592186360569} {:db/id 17592186360570} {:db/id 17592186360571} {:db/id 17592186437273}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case"} :step/id #uuid "8627eaba-93e3-51d5-b350-72ee5af3e635" :step/math-academy-id 30862 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167578}} {:db/id 17592186167578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168062 :tutorial/content "How do we apply the multivariable chain rule if the intermediate variables are also dependent on two variables? 

For example, suppose we have

$$
f = f(x,y), \qquad x=g(s,t), \qquad y=h(s,t).
$$

How do we compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}?$ 

First, let's construct a tree diagram.

![](images/ca/ca524eda2e6be3354fcb72bed52fcaf22257073c3228d74850f8226f9ef0af6f.png)

Now, since we're interested in $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s},$ we highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $s:$

![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

If we keep $t$ fixed and differentiate $f$ with respect to $s,$ then according to the chain rule for two intermediate variables and one independent variable, we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}.
$$

Similarly, if we wanted to compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ we would highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

Keeping $s$ fixed and differentiating $f$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58d189b1-31fb-5b1b-bc4c-cff6be5e2f7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4958 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "2ffafece-1c0b-50f7-a3b1-e1b2d1bada36" :step/math-academy-id 30894 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167575}} {:db/id 17592186167575 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166749 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166587 :question/id #uuid "1491963b-fbd8-57fa-bdde-f2d6705fbb83" :question/math-academy-id "e-8258"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f26d941b-b4b4-591e-b7e0-ae4bbf81e94b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167311} {:db/id 17592186167325} {:db/id 17592186284668} {:db/id 17592186284669} {:db/id 17592186323886} {:db/id 17592186360483} {:db/id 17592186360484} {:db/id 17592186378038} {:db/id 17592186385363} {:db/id 17592186385824} {:db/id 17592186437272}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "60b2ea1e-4b9a-5557-99ae-a83016e785a6" :step/math-academy-id 30863 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167579}} {:db/id 17592186167579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168063 :tutorial/content "We can generalize the chain rule to a multivariable function containing an arbitrary number of intermediate and independent variables.

Consider the multivariable function 

$$
f = f(x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

with $m$ independent variables and, for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\},$ the variable 

$$
x_i = g_i(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)
$$

is a differentiable function of $n$ independent variables. Then,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial t_j} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial t_j} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_m}{\partial t_j}
$$

for $j \in \{1,2,\ldots, n\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba7d2a4-05a6-5e62-8035-2610239633c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4959 :tutorial/title "The Generalized Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "9731a04f-c2d1-5342-b940-0313b71ca1eb" :step/math-academy-id 30895 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167576}} {:db/id 17592186167576 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166750 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166588 :question/id #uuid "e535fe44-a3cb-5c11-831c-118b90582c0d" :question/math-academy-id "e-8259"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71c243ca-5d46-58d2-bd16-28075c04d2db" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167328} {:db/id 17592186167329} {:db/id 17592186284670} {:db/id 17592186323885} {:db/id 17592186360507} {:db/id 17592186360508} {:db/id 17592186360509} {:db/id 17592186360510} {:db/id 17592186360511} {:db/id 17592186383614} {:db/id 17592186385370} {:db/id 17592186420996}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "26ddca41-ae16-5395-ae11-41c4d70303c6" :step/math-academy-id 30864} {:db/id 17592186168061 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for single variable functions $f=f(x)$ and $x=x(t)$ states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.
$$

Let's now suppose that $f = f(x,y),$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$ are single-variable functions. How do we find $\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d t}$ in this case?

The functions $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are known as **intermediate variables.** They are independent variables for the function $f(x,y),$ but are themselves dependent on the variable $t.$

One way to consider how $f(x,y)$ depends on $t$ is to draw a tree diagram.

Starting with $f(x,y),$ we draw a branch for each intermediate variable. Then, we draw a branch for both $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ which are both dependent on the variable $t.$

![](images/cd/cdc47e038ecaba62ae612a0ac0bc07067af232353fc4fc169bf4be57b3abbd1f.png)

We then label each branch with the derivative describing how the function changes due to a change in the variable. 

![](images/ec/ece6012e358b5b6920395df88acd8d7037a7b15bed1add1220365ba72bd24cbd.png)

Then, traversing each branch, we compute the product of the derivatives along each branch and place the result at the end of the branch.

![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

Finally, to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t},$ we sum the results for each branch:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}
 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

This result is called the **multivariable chain rule**." :tutorial/id #uuid "80ad8a26-7d43-52d6-b0ba-e1d04283e5ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4957 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186168062 :tutorial/content "How do we apply the multivariable chain rule if the intermediate variables are also dependent on two variables? 

For example, suppose we have

$$
f = f(x,y), \qquad x=g(s,t), \qquad y=h(s,t).
$$

How do we compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}?$ 

First, let's construct a tree diagram.

![](images/ca/ca524eda2e6be3354fcb72bed52fcaf22257073c3228d74850f8226f9ef0af6f.png)

Now, since we're interested in $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s},$ we highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $s:$

![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

If we keep $t$ fixed and differentiate $f$ with respect to $s,$ then according to the chain rule for two intermediate variables and one independent variable, we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}.
$$

Similarly, if we wanted to compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ we would highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

Keeping $s$ fixed and differentiating $f$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58d189b1-31fb-5b1b-bc4c-cff6be5e2f7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4958 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Two Independent Variables"} {:db/id 17592186168063 :tutorial/content "We can generalize the chain rule to a multivariable function containing an arbitrary number of intermediate and independent variables.

Consider the multivariable function 

$$
f = f(x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

with $m$ independent variables and, for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\},$ the variable 

$$
x_i = g_i(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)
$$

is a differentiable function of $n$ independent variables. Then,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial t_j} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial t_j} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_m}{\partial t_j}
$$

for $j \in \{1,2,\ldots, n\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba7d2a4-05a6-5e62-8035-2610239633c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4959 :tutorial/title "The Generalized Multivariable Chain Rule"} {:db/id 17592186168088 :tutorial/content "There is a special case of the multivariable chain rule when $f=f(x,y)$ and $y=g(x).$ 

Notice that $x$ is an independent variable here. Therefore, the chain rule becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}}_{⏟}}_{1}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "44effd03-02e7-5eb1-8732-ee1522afa147" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5184 :tutorial/title "A Special Case of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186420998} :activity/id #uuid "844676a2-0a90-5f03-a7c1-22515b371e49" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050031 :topic/id #uuid "27615ef6-ec0e-5e91-b58b-24b70dc01a09" :topic/math-academy-id 3173} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186420997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(2t-1)" :db/id 17592186355012} {:answer/id #uuid "392f1f1c-1dad-5e72-b1e4-40cf201a767c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}t(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355179} {:answer/id #uuid "869f5f73-0c65-5003-ade6-8eeef3e8b4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355855} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0fe58-16c4-5d79-ab11-4893e9ff089a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(s-1)" :db/id 17592186356369} {:answer/id #uuid "fa6ace28-41b6-5a2e-8b64-9dee698d22fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(t-1)" :db/id 17592186356853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356853} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314b903-87e4-5c8c-a8db-703d520d008b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1e3cf4a-155f-587d-ba03-cc737759407e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94448" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y,$ where $x=2st$ and $y={s}^{2}t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2cf7698e-82a3-5979-93cb-d2edffbb99d7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421000}} {:db/id 17592186420998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323885 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a9a8991-24fd-50f9-8941-a329e3133c45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+10{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186321230} {:answer/id #uuid "84b790fb-dce2-5ea5-9fbd-fb66967b78c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-20s\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322195} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1f027a-f67b-5d1f-b407-9ee3b85b3667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322598} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfc905-fde6-54a5-83ad-c5fa1e325d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322709} {:answer/id #uuid "f675ee7a-8c5d-5a9a-90cb-d0e4dd971fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-15s\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186323079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322709} :answer-field/id #uuid "af1de9ae-38d9-5d66-a275-9fc76c319cbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bd5b5db6-0961-5b1c-8f50-24c2f4348bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37132" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6a9db776-142d-5ace-9b62-834d4e4b6a63" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421001}} {:db/id 17592186420999 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284667 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186281709} {:answer/id #uuid "49b2d0a3-8640-5928-a7d2-f8a14102a68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))" :db/id 17592186282314} {:answer/id #uuid "e8a1e1c7-9e8a-5f17-9500-4d7507d44b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283715} {:answer/id #uuid "efd819c9-60d2-5826-9266-3dba4a49aaec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283779} {:answer/id #uuid "f5de75cd-c44e-5baf-9f07-d98f3333edab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186283839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282314} :answer-field/id #uuid "d658fcd0-7d37-5a87-a5b6-42706ffef583" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cdba7da9-8893-51f6-a38d-eccc847b176c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170670" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+{c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}st+{c}_{3}s{t}^{4},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "926bef20-92d0-5cd4-928e-9a8dd40763b1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420997}}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186420989} {:db/id 17592186420998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323885 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a9a8991-24fd-50f9-8941-a329e3133c45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+10{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186321230} {:answer/id #uuid "84b790fb-dce2-5ea5-9fbd-fb66967b78c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-20s\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322195} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1f027a-f67b-5d1f-b407-9ee3b85b3667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322598} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfc905-fde6-54a5-83ad-c5fa1e325d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322709} {:answer/id #uuid "f675ee7a-8c5d-5a9a-90cb-d0e4dd971fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-15s\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186323079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322709} :answer-field/id #uuid "af1de9ae-38d9-5d66-a275-9fc76c319cbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bd5b5db6-0961-5b1c-8f50-24c2f4348bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37132" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6a9db776-142d-5ace-9b62-834d4e4b6a63" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421001}} {:db/id 17592186420997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(2t-1)" :db/id 17592186355012} {:answer/id #uuid "392f1f1c-1dad-5e72-b1e4-40cf201a767c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}t(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355179} {:answer/id #uuid "869f5f73-0c65-5003-ade6-8eeef3e8b4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355855} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0fe58-16c4-5d79-ab11-4893e9ff089a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(s-1)" :db/id 17592186356369} {:answer/id #uuid "fa6ace28-41b6-5a2e-8b64-9dee698d22fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(t-1)" :db/id 17592186356853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356853} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314b903-87e4-5c8c-a8db-703d520d008b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1e3cf4a-155f-587d-ba03-cc737759407e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94448" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y,$ where $x=2st$ and $y={s}^{2}t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2cf7698e-82a3-5979-93cb-d2edffbb99d7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421000}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id "f22c7a35-af74-59c8-b71b-cae8347ea97d" :question/math-academy-id "q-37206" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+{z}^{2},$ where $x={s}^{2}+{t}^{2},$ $y=\frac{s}{t}$ and $z=s{t}^{2}.$ Given that

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+{c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}st+{c}_{3}s{t}^{4},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "926bef20-92d0-5cd4-928e-9a8dd40763b1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420997}} {:db/id 17592186420999 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284667 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186281709} {:answer/id #uuid "49b2d0a3-8640-5928-a7d2-f8a14102a68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))" :db/id 17592186282314} {:answer/id #uuid "e8a1e1c7-9e8a-5f17-9500-4d7507d44b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283715} {:answer/id #uuid "efd819c9-60d2-5826-9266-3dba4a49aaec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283779} {:answer/id #uuid "f5de75cd-c44e-5baf-9f07-d98f3333edab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186283839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282314} :answer-field/id #uuid "d658fcd0-7d37-5a87-a5b6-42706ffef583" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cdba7da9-8893-51f6-a38d-eccc847b176c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170670" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ef0c797-03b2-58eb-8a37-83236f476fe8"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

$$

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)=2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $3.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435719 :question/id #uuid "e7130a2f-a2af-518c-8ac7-89bf1a4dc82f" :question/math-academy-id "q-343673"} {:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $1.$ Therefore,
$\omega =1.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =1$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(2D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(2C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]+t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2D\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2C\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only solution I matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186231576 :question/id #uuid "a2dc0571-7d63-58c4-a7e9-b264e1dac3a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-343760" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cac41120-247d-5821-b7f6-b342dbcf8f18" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8588f05c-f259-5f6f-95a4-ba743efb8633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186230323} {:answer/id #uuid "87e2a5ac-5e6b-5176-ada3-76165f3827b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186230324} {:answer/id #uuid "bd0f684b-31be-53dd-959a-4c693200fbd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186230325} {:answer/id #uuid "ebbe1595-b0a0-5005-89d3-b1a66671386d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186230326} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad71e63-ab40-5319-b40d-20fec2c9d4de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186230327}] :answer-field/id #uuid "e6c1fc5b-ecb6-509b-ab8e-ba64d464ed59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186230322}] :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. $$
y''+\omega^2y=f(t),
$$

where $\omega$ is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation $y''+\omega^2y=0$ and $y_p$ is any particular solution to the full equation.

Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}$

Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form

$$
f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),
$$

so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

A sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ would duplicate $y_c,$ so at resonance we multiply by $t$ and use a trial of the form

$$
y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

To determine $C$ and $D,$ we first compute derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+t(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t))-t{\omega }^{2}(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the equation, we have that the $t$-terms cancel out, and we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}{y}_{p}=2\omega D\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)-2\omega C\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we need $y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),$ equating coefficients gives

$$
2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},
$$

so a standard resonant particular solution is

$$
y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

So, when $f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)$ and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b19a33b7-fd81-538c-8139-d44653c47533" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14777 :tutorial/title "General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "35c65152-fe66-57ca-8c82-a01849b005d7" :step/math-academy-id 612654 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231834}} {:db/id 17592186231834 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231429 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231295 :question/id #uuid "f41473ff-05a6-5f3e-ae5b-0584810aa0dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-21878"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cac41120-247d-5821-b7f6-b342dbcf8f18" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231571} {:db/id 17592186231576} {:db/id 17592186317427} {:db/id 17592186317429} {:db/id 17592186317430} {:db/id 17592186317431} {:db/id 17592186317432} {:db/id 17592186317433} {:db/id 17592186427272} {:db/id 17592186435718} {:db/id 17592186435720} {:db/id 17592186442740}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations"} :step/id #uuid "eb6f14ff-8487-50a4-a45b-1ff02e60483d" :step/math-academy-id 612655 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231835}} {:db/id 17592186231835 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231988 :tutorial/content "Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of $t$). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases *without bound*.

For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator

$$
y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).
$$

The complementary solution is of the form $y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),$ the natural frequency of the system is $\omega = 3,$ and the forcing frequency is also $3.$ Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

Since the forcing term $\sin(3t)$ duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by $t.$ We try a solution of the form $y_p = t(C\cos(3t) + D\sin(3t)).$

Calculating the derivatives of $y_p,$ substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of $\sin(3t)$ and $\cos(3t)$ yields $C=-\dfrac16$ and $D=0.$ So, the particular solution is of the form

$$
y_p = -\dfrac{t}{6}\cos(3t).
$$

Notice that this solution grows larger as $t$ increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.

In real systems, perfectly *unbounded growth* does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude. Even so, forcing near the natural frequency can still produce very large oscillations, which is why resonance is important in engineering design." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f439c3c-eac7-5d41-a8b1-fcbe2eb8d44b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14778 :tutorial/title "Practical Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "d14184e9-93ef-5eca-99aa-b25660380309" :step/math-academy-id 612658}] :activity/title "Resonance in Vibrating Systems" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231520} {:db/id 17592186231830 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231985 :tutorial/content "A standard vibrating system under an external force ![](images/f6/f6ec0c498eee67c8bceaf8cf937f9b77f6395bd4ad28df6da30ca42622366f99.svg) looks like

$$
y''+\omega^2y=f(t),
$$

where $\omega$ is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation $y''+\omega^2y=0$ and $y_p$ is any particular solution to the full equation.

Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

1\. $y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}$

2\. $y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}$

3\. $y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}$

Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form

$$
f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),
$$

so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega.$

A sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega$ would duplicate $y_c,$ so at resonance we multiply by $t$ and use a trial of the form

$$
y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

To determine $C$ and $D,$ we first compute derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+t(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & =2(-C\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)+D\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t))-t{\omega }^{2}(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the equation, we have that the $t$-terms cancel out, and we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}{y}_{p}=2\omega D\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)-2\omega C\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we need $y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),$ equating coefficients gives

$$
2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},
$$

so a standard resonant particular solution is

$$
y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).
$$

So, when $f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)$ and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b19a33b7-fd81-538c-8139-d44653c47533" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14777 :tutorial/title "General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "35c65152-fe66-57ca-8c82-a01849b005d7" :step/math-academy-id 612654 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231834}} {:db/id 17592186231987 :tutorial/content "Consider an undamped forced oscillator,

In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of $t$). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases *without bound*.

For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator

$$
y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).
$$

The complementary solution is of the form $y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),$ the natural frequency of the system is $\omega = 3,$ and the forcing frequency is also $3.$ Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

Since the forcing term $\sin(3t)$ duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by $t.$ We try a solution of the form $y_p = t(C\cos(3t) + D\sin(3t)).$

Calculating the derivatives of $y_p,$ substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of $\sin(3t)$ and $\cos(3t)$ yields $C=-\dfrac16$ and $D=0.$ So, the particular solution is of the form

$$
y_p = -\dfrac{t}{6}\cos(3t).
$$

Notice that this solution grows larger as $t$ increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.

In real systems, perfectly *unbounded growth* does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude. Even so, forcing near the natural frequency can still produce very large oscillations, which is why resonance is important in engineering design." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f439c3c-eac7-5d41-a8b1-fcbe2eb8d44b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14778 :tutorial/title "Practical Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "d14184e9-93ef-5eca-99aa-b25660380309" :step/math-academy-id 612658} {:db/id 17592186231988 :tutorial/content "Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$

$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2595439f-c010-51c2-987d-b6e986cd13da" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441794}} {:db/id 17592186441793 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317422 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cca9f77e-1eac-5dd3-b2b8-a6a15bf83357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{18}{5}" :db/id 17592186316277} {:answer/id #uuid "282a52cc-8658-5a56-b555-abd92b1826a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.6" :db/id 17592186441790}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186316277} :answer-field/id #uuid "6fa88ca7-4486-52c4-a8ca-dfdd856acf42" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186316816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7756f2f0-f8ff-5a38-a573-589b8cc562e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343691" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$

$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-1$ and $D=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$

$$

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Only solution III matches the forms above.

:question/math-academy-id "q-343753" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-1$ and $D=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Only solution III matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."} :step/id #uuid "c0f6cdf0-cd51-5bdc-9771-44211b216c7d"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14290d8c-e867-59b8-af1c-fccb11ec1cd5" :answer/type The external force is $f(t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $2.$ Therefore,
$\omega =2.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =2$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[4(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)]+4t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 4D\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4C\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =-7\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{7}{4}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{7}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$

Only solutions I and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} :step/id #uuid "102631d9-03a3-5a77-8b43-d3ebf3037f1b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442743}} {:db/id 17592186442742 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317422 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cca9f77e-1eac-5dd3-b2b8-a6a15bf83357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{18}{5}" :db/id 17592186316277} {:answer/id #uuid "282a52cc-8658-5a56-b555-abd92b1826a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.6" :db/id 17592186441790}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186316277} :answer-field/id #uuid "6fa88ca7-4486-52c4-a8ca-dfdd856acf42" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186316816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7756f2f0-f8ff-5a38-a573-589b8cc562e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-343691" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+(4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)-2).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)-1).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)-1)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=5(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)-1)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $3.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{18}{5}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5ee37f4e-428d-5c80-b898-6258e65e6514" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442744}} {:db/id 17592186442743 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317431 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f62d1759-0498-58c4-ab55-caa874c6319e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186467268} {:answer/id #uuid "d1649d8f-ee2f-5778-b299-fa2795a13fbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186467269}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186467269} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d72ca48-f0c0-538a-84c8-10419eca178e" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468355} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ce9985f7-ada6-59aa-9213-ea46b2f0103a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186467270} {:answer/id #uuid "2b5c8f3b-63a5-5160-a7b3-de3cdcbe35f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186467271}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186467271} :answer-field/id #uuid "c70a8fc2-cc6d-5e11-8840-935b2c760d12" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468356} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "891fbb34-02a0-5178-be8c-59a9c40ccee8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186467272} {:answer/id #uuid "b5910d95-689b-5498-970e-cb215a933405" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186467273}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186467273} :answer-field/id #uuid "1174ed98-32d3-5eef-b1f3-eb94a6edeefc" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186468357}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ceda7f80-0812-553b-8a96-78a8d37d4fb1" :question/math-academy-id "q-343761" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)=2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $3.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "83ab17b5-350b-529d-97cb-ee01d416ef71" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442745}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f62d1759-0498-58c4-ab55-caa874c6319e" :answer/type {:db/id $$

mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{4}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(13-\frac{5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{34}{3} \\  & =\frac{17M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{17}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{17}{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198665 :question/id #uuid "2496e287-b250-5877-a40c-af954399de62" :question/math-academy-id "q-163612" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e41b76a-dabb-5807-a6bb-5779e0a43c8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186278869} {:answer/id #uuid "59d4646c-a8cc-5cc4-8c20-a790ad2f4d3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}" :db/id 17592186279413} {:answer/id #uuid "74959f37-361c-597f-97f4-79fda9c4ad64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}" :db/id 17592186279642} {:answer/id #uuid "ed79e371-e80a-5031-880e-b39448d43e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186280675} {:answer/id #uuid "ee046b1f-ca21-54a9-88ec-7eeb4e214626" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186280677}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280675} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee676f82-5c11-53e9-9b1a-845255b4b041" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281256}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,4\le y\le 6\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{4}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{4}^{6}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{4}^{6}\frac{1}{3}(1-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{4}^{6}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}[y]_{4}^{6} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(6-4) \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186235554 :question/id #uuid "12d7be9e-b12c-5440-971b-269b8c57642f" :question/math-academy-id "q-169104"} {:db/id 17592186281676 :question/id #uuid "c58b6231-e237-5de8-8e27-d0ade4f5cce7" :question/math-academy-id "q-163576" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198417 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2bfe2e3e-9d7b-5c53-8de8-2717237d3e9c" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Radius of Gyration of a Uniform Rectangular Laminar"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28052605-ef85-5d61-b60d-35c652016958" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186278950} {:answer/id #uuid "30e535dc-d841-51b2-9346-6dd8f8151f9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}" :db/id 17592186279019} {:answer/id #uuid "7d4a7fcf-e348-50c3-a268-aaa5fcf0d810" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}" :db/id 17592186279712} {:answer/id #uuid "cd62681a-f336-57f7-9271-562c7877f73a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}" :db/id 17592186280402} {:answer/id #uuid "e5cb850d-af3a-58fe-9a74-754886c3ca4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186280620}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e5cb850d-af3a-58fe-9a74-754886c3ca4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186280620} :answer-field/id #uuid "2fb299df-44bd-5725-bf66-0524bf139842" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186280921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(8-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 3=3.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(1+9) \\  & =\frac{10M}{3}.\end{aligned}

Finally,

$$

$D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{7}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{7}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(7+9-\frac{7}{3}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{40}{3} \\  & =\frac{20M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{20}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{20}{3}}=2\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435469 :question/id #uuid "07899bf0-acd5-5cb5-8654-0b2936590b7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163577"} {:db/id 17592186435471 :question/id #uuid "464dc60e-dfa3-5c24-8df3-bdca1e567180" :question/math-academy-id "q-163608"} {:db/id 17592186435472 :question/id #uuid "9f4fdbea-b5e1-5c4f-b10b-d88e66b48be2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163610"} {:db/id 17592186435473 :question/id #uuid "a8f6939e-ee8d-5d31-921b-202a2621754c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163581"} {:db/id 17592186435475 :question/id #uuid "cba3666c-1980-5c09-82de-e7dd19c40b69" :question/math-academy-id "q-163575"} {:db/id 17592186444168 :question/id #uuid "4a051470-22b3-5741-85c9-94876b2374fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-163606" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "020395fa-1c94-56f4-b0cf-6b542584a05e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{21}" :db/id 17592186444156} {:answer/id #uuid "4e9fa620-f201-58e2-aec9-4998cb5b396c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{17}}{3}" :db/id 17592186444159} {:answer/id #uuid "61c6c170-edd9-5422-8928-2559bb6d8200" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{34}{3}}" :db/id 17592186444160} {:answer/id #uuid "7f05bbf6-f47e-5bba-ae07-b44dd179c296" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{61}{2}}" :db/id 17592186444162} {:answer/id #uuid "aed2bb04-ea3b-5b55-b733-92f0f589ec24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{17}" :db/id 17592186444164}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444160} :answer-field/id #uuid "364a1bfa-3c03-5519-b8cb-713056748a8b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region

${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by

where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 2=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{64}{3}+4{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}21+3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[21y+{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(63+27-21-1) \\  & =\frac{M}{6}\cdot 68 \\  & =\frac{34M}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{34}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{34}{3}}.

${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 3=9.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{9}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}(\frac{64}{3}-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}21\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}[y]_{2}^{5} \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}(5-2) \\  & =7M.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=7\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{7}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198419 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198061 :question/id #uuid "fa3e8249-cb9f-50f6-a56f-6f311d101de6" :question/math-academy-id "e-12495"} :knowledge-point/id A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
